children: A Bank of Japan policy board member called for a flexible approach to raising interest rates, saying the inflation target has nearly been met and the risk of prices overheating is rising.

In a speech to business leaders in Hokkaido on Wednesday, Hajime Takata said that this year represents a "regime change," in which rate hikes aren't carried out at a fixed pace, but instead will be "conducted in a nimble and data-dependent manner in response to the domestic price and economic environment, particularly reflecting overseas trends."

Takata, seen as one of the BOJ board's most hawkish members, proposed raising the benchmark rate to 1.25% at its July meeting. The proposal was defeated in an 8-1 vote, leaving the rate at 1%, where it has stood since June.

With underlying inflation nearing the BOJ's 2% target, the central bank needs to move the policy rate closer to a level that is neither stimulative nor restrictive to the economy to avoid second-round effects on price growth, Takata said.
Investors appear to agree, with the overnight index swap market pricing in a 94% chance of a September move.

The yen's continued weakness against the dollar has added to that conviction, with many seeing faster tightening by the BOJ--which would narrow the rate gap with the U.S.--as an effective way to prop up the currency after repeated interventions in the foreign-exchange market have had limited impact.
Expectations for an imminent rate hike have heightened as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has repeatedly voiced concerns about an undervalued yen and its impact on global market stability.

Speaking with Ueda on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance leaders meeting on Sunday, Bessent expressed his support for Japan's decisive steps to address the yen's undervaluation and noted the currency's role in driving domestic inflation, a Treasury statement showed.
Economists say it is difficult for Japan to ignore tacit U.S. pressure to raise rates, given the importance of the alliance between the two countries.
